title: Birational locally finitely presented morphisms restrict to an isomorphism of dense opens
statement: Let $f:Y\to X$ be a morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme] that is locally of finite presentation [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. Suppose $X$ and $Y$ have finitely many irreducible components [def-weil-irreducible-components]. Assume $f$ maps the generic points of the irreducible components of $Y$ bijectively onto those of $X$ [def-sc-generic-point], and for every such generic point $\eta$ of $Y$ the induced homomorphism $\mathcal O_{X,f(\eta)}\to\mathcal O_{Y,\eta}$ is an isomorphism [def-weil-locally-ringed-space-morphism]. Then there are dense open subschemes $U\subseteq Y$ and $V\subseteq X$ [def-weil-open-immersion] such that $f(U)\subseteq V$ and the restriction $f|_U:U\to V$ is an isomorphism. No separatedness or reducedness hypothesis is imposed; the conclusion does not assert that $U=f^{-1}(V)$.

source.place: Tag 0BAC, lemma-birational-birational, locally-of-finite-presentation alternative (2); birational as in Definition 01RO (definition-birational), morphisms.tex lines 12980-12998.

proof.text: If there are no irreducible components, both schemes are empty and we take $U=Y$, $V=X$. Otherwise enumerate the component generic points as $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_r$ in $Y$ and $\xi_i=f(\eta_i)$ in $X$, using the assumed bijection. By sobriety their closures are exactly the respective components $Y_i$ and $X_i$. Set $Y_i^\circ=Y\setminus\bigcup_{j\ne i}Y_j$ and $X_i^\circ=X\setminus\bigcup_{j\ne i}X_j$. These are open because the component families are finite. Each contains its own generic point: membership of $\eta_i$ in another closed component would force $Y_i\subseteq Y_j$, contrary to maximality; the same argument applies to $X$. They are pairwise disjoint and contained in their respective components. Every nonempty open subset of $Y_i^\circ$ contains $\eta_i$: its complement in $Y_i$ is closed and would contain the closure of $\eta_i$ if it contained $\eta_i$. Thus $\eta_i$ remains generic on every neighbourhood inside $Y_i^\circ$, and likewise for $\xi_i$.

source.place: Tag 0BAC, lemma-birational-birational, first sentence: reduction to irreducible schemes, with the omitted finite-component reduction written out.

proof.text: For each $i$, choose an affine open $V_i^0=\operatorname{Spec}B\subseteq X_i^\circ$ containing $\xi_i$. Choose an affine open $U_i^0=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq Y_i^\circ\cap f^{-1}(V_i^0)$ containing $\eta_i$; the latter open contains $\eta_i$ since $f(\eta_i)=\xi_i$. The affine-chart square identifies this restriction of $f$ with $\operatorname{Spec}\varphi$ for its induced ring map $\varphi:B\to A$. Both affine spectra have a generic point for the whole space by Step 1, hence are irreducible: two nonempty opens both contain that point. The component/minimal-prime description of spectra therefore gives unique minimal primes $\mathfrak q$ of $B$ and $\mathfrak p$ of $A$, representing $\xi_i$ and $\eta_i$. Carry out Steps 3--6 for each $i$ with these rings.

The map on affine points gives $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak p)=\mathfrak q$. The affine stalk-map formula identifies the stipulated generic local-ring isomorphism with the induced map $B_{\mathfrak q}\to A_{\mathfrak p}$. Apply [lem-sfb-birational-generic-localization]: its unique-minimal-prime and contraction hypotheses were established in Step 2 and the first sentence here. Consequently the canonical map $B_{\mathfrak q}\to A_{\mathfrak q}=\varphi(B\setminus\mathfrak q)^{-1}A$ is an isomorphism. Here and below $A_g$ means localization of $A$ at $\varphi(g)$.

The affine-chart finite-presentation theorem applied directly to $f,U_i^0,V_i^0$ gives $A\cong B[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/(h_1,\ldots,h_m)$; let $x_j$ be the images of the variables. Surjectivity of $B_{\mathfrak q}	o A_{\mathfrak q}$ writes $x_j/1=\varphi(b_j)/\varphi(s_j)$ for some $s_j
otin\mathfrak q$. The equality criterion for fractions supplies $s_j^\prime
otin\mathfrak q$ with $\varphi(s_j^\prime)(\varphi(b_j)-\varphi(s_j)x_j)=0$ in $A$. Put $g=\prod_j s_js_j^\prime
otin\mathfrak q$ (empty product $1$). Every factor becomes a unit in $B_g$ and $A_g$, so $x_j=\varphi(b_j)/\varphi(s_j)$ in $A_g$. The map $B_g	o A_g$ is surjective: $A_g$ is generated as a ring by the images of $B$, the $x_j$, and $\varphi(g)^{-1}$, all now in its image.

source.place: Tag 0BAC, lemma-birational-birational, finite-generator denominator argument before alternative (2).

proof.text: Localizing the displayed presentation gives $A_g\cong B_g[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/(h_1,\ldots,h_m)$: a map from either ring into any $B_g$-algebra amounts to choosing $n$ elements satisfying the same relations. Thus $A_g$ is finitely presented over $B_g$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-presentation-surjection-kernel-fg] with coefficient ring $B_g$, target $A_g$, and zero polynomial variables, to obtain finitely many generators $c_1,\ldots,c_a$ of $J=\ker(B_g\to A_g)$. Write $c_j=b_j/g^{e_j}$. Its image in $A_{\mathfrak q}$ is zero, and injectivity in Step 3 implies $b_j/1=0$ in $B_{\mathfrak q}$. The fraction equality criterion gives $u_j\notin\mathfrak q$ with $u_jb_j=0$ in $B$. Put $h=g\prod_j u_j\notin\mathfrak q$. The map $B_h\to A_h$ remains surjective by the same generators as in Step 4. It is injective as well: if $b/h^e$ maps to zero, then $\varphi(h)^k\varphi(b)=0$ in $A$ for some $k$. Hence $h^kb/1\in J$ inside $B_g$. All $c_j$ vanish in $B_h$, so $h^kb/1=0$ there; since $h$ is a unit, $b/h^e=0$. We have an isomorphism $B_h\xrightarrow{\sim}A_h$.

source.place: Tag 0BAC, lemma-birational-birational, proof of alternative (2); Tag 00R2, algebra-lemma-finite-presentation-independent, for the finitely generated kernel.

proof.text: Let $V_i=D(h)\subseteq V_i^0$ and $U_i=D(\varphi(h))\subseteq U_i^0$. Principal-localization open immersions identify these with $\operatorname{Spec}B_h$ and $\operatorname{Spec}A_h$. The fraction map $B_h\to A_h$ extends $\varphi$ and commutes with localization maps; applying the contravariant functor $\operatorname{Spec}$ gives the corresponding commutative square. Thus $f|_{U_i}:U_i\to V_i$ is precisely $\operatorname{Spec}(B_h\to A_h)$. Functoriality applied to the inverse ring isomorphism from Step 5 makes this restriction an isomorphism. The opens contain $\xi_i$ and $\eta_i$, respectively, since $h\notin\mathfrak q$ and $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak p)=\mathfrak q$. Each $U_i$ remains inside $Y_i^\circ$ and each $V_i$ inside $X_i^\circ$.

source.place: Tag 0BAC, lemma-birational-birational, conclusion of the affine argument; Tag 01I3, schemes-lemma-standard-open-affine.

proof.text: Set $U=\bigcup_iU_i$ and $V=\bigcup_iV_i$. The pairwise disjoint open pieces identify the restricted map $f|_U$ with the piecewise isomorphisms $U_i\to V_i$. Explicitly its inverse sends a point of $V_i$ by the inverse of this isomorphism. It is continuous since the $V_i$ form an open partition. On any open $W\subseteq V$, the sheaf axiom for the disjoint cover $W=\coprod_i(W\cap V_i)$ identifies sections with the product of the section rings on the pieces (the overlaps are empty); the inverse sheaf maps on the pieces give inverse ring maps on these products, compatible with restrictions. These define the inverse morphism of locally ringed spaces, since its maps on local rings are the local inverses. Hence $f|_U:U\to V$ is an isomorphism of open subschemes. Finally $U$ contains every $\eta_i$, so its closure contains every $Y_i=\overline{\{\eta_i\}}$, and hence all of $Y$; similarly $V$ is dense in $X$. The desired source open is the union of the selected $U_i$, which need not exhaust $f^{-1}(V)$.
